diagnosis: Generated forecasts frequently miss the true next news due to: (1) failing to anticipate topic drift away from the central dispute toward corporate financial results, unrelated local news, or competitive dynamics; (2) over-committing to concrete policy actions or corporate investments that are not imminent, while true news tends to come from secondary actors (industry associations, lawmakers) or procedural steps; (3) under-predicting escalation (e.g., warnings, cancellations, public criticism) when the latest articles show tension or defensive posturing. These errors are not consistently optimistic or pessimistic but reflect over-attachment to a narrow narrative and premature specificity about outcomes.
suggestions: When the latest articles depict a diplomatic stalemate, internal corporate spat, or defensive posturing, do not assume the next headline will advance the same sub-story; treat topic drift as the default expectation—the next news may be about a different company's financials, an unrelated local event, or a competitive shift (e.g., EV market threats) that does not directly address the dispute.

Eschew predicting concrete government actions (e.g., invoking regulations, issuing specific ministerial statements) or corporate investments unless the latest article provides a firm deadline or explicit imminent plan; instead, anchor forecasts on statements from secondary actors (industry associations, lawmakers, analysts) or factual updates on existing procedural steps (e.g., hearing occurs, meeting called) without assigning a specific outcome.

If the historical trajectory includes accusations, canceled visits, or public warnings, anticipate that the next newsworthy development may be an escalation from a previously peripheral actor (e.g., a corporate warning with a deadline, a diplomatic demand) rather than a de-escalation or collaborative move; avoid predicting diplomatic progress unless the latest article explicitly signals goodwill gestures.
